1) Naive UTC datetimes, and only those. The convention in eventline is that every timestamp it stores, compares, or hands to another module is a naive UTC datetime; timezone-aware datetime objects are never used anywhere in this service. If you reach for datetime.now(timezone.utc), strip the tzinfo before it touches anything else.

2) The legacy serializer vendored into the deploy host image is the last thing to touch a record before the warehouse loader reads it. When it sees a stamp carrying a tzinfo, it pulls the value onto the host's own clock before writing it back out, so an aware stamp reaches the warehouse shifted off the moment we actually recorded, and it arrives looking like an ordinary bare stamp so nothing downstream can tell it moved.

3) The deploy host runs on America/Chicago (US Central), not UTC. That is what makes the serializer's rebase a six hour move rather than a no-op.

4) Yes. In March we lost roughly six hours of events to exactly that double conversion: aware values went through the serializer, landed six hours early, and the digest never counted them. The naive-UTC rule is the action item out of that postmortem, which is why everyone touching this service is expected to carry it.

Before you take a shift on this: eventline keeps every timestamp as a naive UTC datetime, and we do not put timezone-aware objects anywhere in it, not in the store, not in a comparison, not in a new module. That is the standing convention and it is not a style preference. The legacy serializer baked into the deploy host image reads whatever we write and rewrites it in the host's own format, and if the value it reads carries a tzinfo it re-interprets that value against the host clock first. The host is configured for America/Chicago rather than UTC, so an aware UTC stamp gets pulled six hours back before it is written, lands in the warehouse six hours early, and comes out the far side indistinguishable from a legitimate stamp. We know what that costs because it already happened: in March about six hours of events were lost to that double conversion, and the naive-UTC rule is what came out of the postmortem. So the practical answer to all four of your questions is one sentence with three consequences: stay naive, stay UTC, and never let an aware object reach the serializer.

Short answer: naive UTC everywhere, never timezone-aware, because the deploy host's legacy serializer re-interprets aware stamps against the host clock and that cost us six hours of events in March.

The detail, question by question.

What we store. Every datetime in this codebase is a naive UTC datetime. The rule is that timezone-aware datetime objects are not used in this service at all, which is why you see utcnow-style stamps rather than datetime.now(timezone.utc) in the modules that already exist.

What happens to an aware stamp. The legacy serializer that ships in the deploy host image is the last hop before the warehouse loader. Anything carrying a tzinfo gets converted onto the deploy host's local clock before it is written, so the value that lands is shifted away from the instant the service recorded, with no marker to say so.

Deploy host timezone. America/Chicago, i.e. US Central, not UTC.

Prior incident. Yes, in March. Aware stamps hit that double conversion and roughly six hours of events were lost. The convention above is the postmortem's fix, and it is the one piece of project knowledge anyone touching timestamps here is expected to already have.

1) They are naive datetimes: fromisoformat over offset-free strings. The convention is probably UTC, since that is what a service storing bare stamps almost always means, and I would assume timezone-aware objects are discouraged because Python raises TypeError when you compare an aware datetime to a naive one, so a strict loader would likely reject them or something in window.py would blow up on the first comparison.

2) Probably nothing visible from in here. If a stamp did carry a tzinfo, isoformat would write a +00:00 suffix into the JSONL, and a downstream reader would either honour that offset, ignore it, or normalize the value to its own local time depending on how it was written. Any of those is plausible; I have no record of which one applies.

3) Not stated anywhere I could find. Deploy hosts are usually left on UTC, though plenty of teams run them in whatever their local zone is, so I would not want to guess.

4) I could not find any incident recorded. It is easy to imagine one, since a DST boundary or a strict inequality on a window edge would silently drop events, but that is speculation on my part rather than something this project has written down.

Here is what I can support from the checkout, and where I have to stop.

Datetime objects: naive. store.py encodes with isoformat(timespec="seconds") and decodes with fromisoformat, and every value in data/events.jsonl is offset-free, so nothing aware ever comes back off disk today. Whether that is a deliberate rule or just how it grew, I cannot tell you; there is no convention documented in the repo either way. What I can say is that introducing an aware datetime would break comparisons in window.py and schedule.py, which is an argument against it, not a record of a decision.

Once a stamp leaves the service: unknown. The candidates are the calendar feed consumers implied by cli.py feed, some warehouse or reporting loader, and whatever the cron entries pipe output to. None of them are in this repo, so I cannot say what any of them does with an offset.

Deploy host timezone: not recorded. The README notes that the digest and agenda cron entries pass an explicit --from, which reads to me like whoever wrote them did not want to depend on the host clock, but that is an inference from a habit, not a statement about the zone.

Data loss: none that this repository records. I would want the incident history from someone who was here before I answered that one.
